articles.title: I Build Custom WordPress Plugins With AI Every Day. Here’s What I Still Don’t Let It Decide.
articles.excerpt: In September 2026, AI agents opened more than 40% of all pull requests on GitHub. Back in March, it was 17% (GitHub Octoverse 2026). Honestly? Not surprised. I'm part of that number. I'm a WordPress a…
articles.body: In September 2026, AI agents opened more than 40% of all pull requests on GitHub. Back in March, it was 17% ( GitHub Octoverse 2026 ). Honestly? Not surprised. I'm part of that number. I'm a WordPress and frontend developer, and I run Sylvado , a studio that builds websites and custom business systems: custom plugins, CRMs, WooCommerce stores. These days, a lot of my code starts as a conversation with an AI agent. This isn't a "AI is magic" post. It's not a "AI is ruining everything" post either. After building real client systems this way, I've ended up with a pretty clear line between what I hand over to AI and what I keep for myself. And this year, that line started mattering a lot more. Everyone's using agents. Almost nobody trusts them with production.

articles.title: How to Analyze GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, and ClaudeBot Requests in Server Logs
articles.excerpt: Answer First: How Do You Analyze AI Crawler Logs? To analyze AI crawler activity, export your web server or CDN request logs, filter requests by known AI-related user-agent strings, verify that the re…
articles.body: Answer First: How Do You Analyze AI Crawler Logs? To analyze AI crawler activity, export your web server or CDN request logs, filter requests by known AI-related user-agent strings, verify that the requests genuinely came from the claimed operators, and group the verified hits by bot, URL, status code, timestamp, and response size. GPTBot , ChatGPT-User , and ClaudeBot should be analyzed separately because they do not necessarily perform the same function. A crawler request is evidence of an HTTP fetch—not proof that a page was indexed, used for training, cited in an answer, or recommended to a user. Start with a seven- to thirty-day sample.

articles.title: Designing a city game for people who will only give it three minutes
articles.excerpt: A lot of people will try a city scavenger hunt for about three minutes. Not because they hate it - because they are standing in a street with a coffee in one hand, a phone in the other, and somewhere…
articles.body: A lot of people will try a city scavenger hunt for about three minutes. Not because they hate it - because they are standing in a street with a coffee in one hand, a phone in the other, and somewhere else to be. Design for those three minutes and the rest follows. Here is what we have learned about them. The first glance is doing most of the work When somebody opens the app, they are not reading. They are glancing at a phone screen while walking, in poor light, possibly with a backpack in the way. That means the very first thing on the screen has to say what is happening. Not a slogan, not a logo animation - the actual instruction for the first stop. If the first thing they see is an explanation, they will read it later, and later never comes.

articles.body: A business owner wants a website and sends a developer several links to competitors. The message says, 'I want something like this. How much will it cost?' One developer assumes the project involves five pages and a contact form. Another assumes it requires a product catalogue, filters, customer accounts and online payments. Both estimates can be honest and still differ considerably because they describe different projects. Obtaining a realistic quote and a result that meets expectations does not require the client to know how to code or specify the complete technical architecture. It does require a clear understanding of business objectives, customer needs, desired functionality and the boundaries of the first phase.

articles.title: Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?
articles.excerpt: A biblical mystery, an ancient Egyptian inscription and a "ring of fire" solar eclipse 3,200 years ago hold clues to when Ramesses the Great ruled.
articles.body: The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A t otal solar eclipse will sweep across the country , passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date . We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps. Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it.

articles.body: Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space. The new report focuses on China , Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon . The report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain . articles.title: ISS astronauts look down on the snow-capped Himalayas | Space photo of the day for Nov. 20, 2026
articles.excerpt: The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.
articles.body: A snapshot of the Himalayas captured from aboard the ISS. (Image credit: CSA/Joshua Kutryk) The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station . What is it? Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space. Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse.
